idiom_name: base class calling overridable methods, or a higher-order function taking the step callbacks
implementation_notes: A class whose concrete method calls this.step() does express the pattern (Node's stream contract is exactly it: a subclass implements _read/_write and the base machinery drives them in a fixed order), but JavaScript has no protected visibility and the underscore prefix is only a naming convention, so the everyday realization is a higher-order function or factory that closes over the step callbacks and returns the algorithm. The base-class form is still justified when the steps need instance state, when the class is a framework hook surface (streams, lifecycle methods, Array.prototype.sort's comparator), and when all subclasses are internal to the library.
pitfalls: There is no protected and no enforcement: a subclass can override the skeleton or forget a step, and the failure appears only at run time, usually as "this.step is not a function".
An underscore-prefixed hook is a convention, not an ABI: renaming it silently changes which method the skeleton calls, and a minifier mangles it unless #private class fields are used.
Passing a step as a bare callback loses `this` (this.step versus () => this.step()), so shared state read inside the step becomes undefined.
